parsed.explanation: The destination state's own regime is strongly protective — a public-accommodations law covering hotels, shops and service providers, no facility ban, mandated gender-neutral single-user restrooms, gender-identity hate-crime coverage, healthcare shield laws and self-ID marker rules. But that state layer cannot displace the national regime the traveller meets first. Entry screening is the operative exposure: passport sex-marker restrictions, halted X-marker processing, case-note tagging where documents raise doubt, and a discretionary lifetime fraud finding, with reported confiscations, stranded travellers and allied-government advisories. Immigration custody carries documented abuse. In-state everyday exposure is low; the border is not, and the border governs the visit.

entry_documents.exposure: National passport rules require birth sex; X-marker processing stopped Feb 2025; officers tag cases and may refuse where documents raise doubt; discretionary lifetime fraud finding; reported confiscations and travellers stranded abroad.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports valid until expiry; fraud finding never automatic and requires four elements with limited waivers; policy under active litigation.
entry_documents.interaction: State self-ID and X-marker rules do not reach federal border screening; the visitor's home-issued document is judged by national officers.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody: trans men report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse. National corrections policies impose hair-cutting, hormone removal and psychiatric substitution; trans prisoner counts no longer reported.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Not documented. The national executive order addressing LGBTQ conditions in prisons was rescinded.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A document discrepancy at entry can convert a traveller into a detainee, moving them from the protective state into national custody.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars federally funded single-sex facility access by identity; facility bans operate in many states, four with criminal exposure, one arrest documented.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This state has no facility ban, requires gender-neutral single-user restrooms since 2018, and its accommodations law covers gender identity.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Facility protection is local; a traveller transiting or crossing into a ban state loses it, and federal buildings follow the national rule.

care_services.exposure: National orders target minors' care and insurance reimbursement; hospitals subpoenaed for under-19 records; care denied in national custody.
care_services.protection: State insurers must cover trans care since 2013; conversion therapy on minors banned; 2023–24 shield laws enforceable against out-of-state action.
care_services.interaction: Shield law protects travel-in care, but national record demands and reimbursement rules can still chill providers serving a minor visitor.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Counterterrorism strategy names 'radically pro-transgender' groups among priorities; DOJ reward memo invokes 'radical gender ideology'; schools investigated over social transition. Advocates allege genocide precursors.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity; this state's hate-crime enhancement and panic-defence repeal; the strategy disclaims targeting mere disagreement.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Rhetoric raises severity if a traveller is swept into any enforcement encounter; state law offers no shield from national security framing.

minors_guardians.exposure: National order directs prosecution of teachers using preferred names; care banned in 27 states; national insurance rules for under-18s; a minor's mismatched document is screened at the border with the guardian.
minors_guardians.protection: This state bans conversion therapy, protects trans students by policy, and covers minors under accommodations and shield laws.
minors_guardians.interaction: A visiting minor is outside the state's school protections; the border and any national custody encounter are the operative risks.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No state-specific violence data in the dossier; national climate hostile; the only documented bathroom arrest occurred in another state.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Gender-identity hate-crime enhancement since 1999, panic defence repealed 2021, public-accommodations coverage, most-protective tier ranking July 2026.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Protections are statutory and untested for visitors; the state cannot control national enforcement actors present at airports and federal property.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No enforcement data for the accommodations or hate-crime provisions; passport policy unresolved in court; protections untested for nonresident complainants.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Statutory remedies exist, shield laws enforceable against out-of-state action, legal-aid guidance on document rules, litigation ongoing.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: A traveller refused entry at the border has no state remedy; in-state service refusals would fall to a state agency with undocumented practice.

anchor_checks.comparison: Veluna imposes a universal birth-sex facility rule with courts rejecting complaints. Here the destination state has no facility ban and mandates gender-neutral single-user restrooms, so in-state exposure is materially lower; but the national entry-document regime supplies a comparable universal exposure at the border that Veluna's profile does not describe, keeping this below a clean protective reading.

Veleda's transport authority performs repeated invasive birth-sex searches with acknowledged but unremedied violations, alongside an accepting society and convicted attackers. The border exposure here is similar in kind and arguably graver in worst case (refusal, stranding, lifetime ineligibility), but narrower in trigger and offset by a stronger, statutorily codified state accommodation regime.

Teravi documents recurring hostile refusals by ferry operators and guesthouses with partial remedies. Here no such refusal pattern is documented and the state's accommodations law is broad, but Teravi's parent regime accepts foreign documents on ordinary terms while this one does not — so the border axis pulls this jurisdiction below Teravi despite stronger in-state law.

Ilvora combines a tolerated traditional role, accepted foreign documents, enforced court-ordered compensation and no organised targeting. This jurisdiction matches some of that in-state but lacks Ilvora's clean entry position: the national document regime, custody record and threat framing are documented exposures Ilvora's profile does not contain.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller experiences two regimes in sequence. Inside the destination state, the operative picture is close to the reduced-risk tier: accommodations law reaches hotels and shops, no facility ban applies, single-user restrooms are gender-neutral, hate-crime enhancement and panic-defence repeal exist, and shield laws protect care travel. But the visit begins and ends at a national border governed by a hostile document regime: birth-sex markers, halted X processing, case-note tagging, discretionary lifetime fraud findings, reported confiscations, and allied-government advisories. Immigration custody, where a document dispute can land a traveller, carries documented forced labour, beatings and sexual abuse. National threat framing raises the severity of any enforcement encounter. The state layer is real but cannot reach the border, custody or federal property, so the combined regime sits mid-scale rather than in the protective tier its state law alone would suggest.
